title: Dependent Prepositions
summary: The fixed prepositions that particular adjectives, verbs and nouns require, and the verbs that must take none at all.

sections.heading: What a Dependent Preposition Is
sections.body:
A **dependent preposition** is the preposition that a particular word demands. It carries almost no meaning of its own: the `in` of `interested in` is not spatial, it is simply the shape the adjective takes when a topic follows.

Because the choice is lexical rather than logical, the pair has to be learned as one item. Translation is no guide, since languages divide the field differently: `depend on` becomes `depend from` or `depend of` under the influence of another language, and neither is possible in English.

The practical habit is to record new vocabulary with its preposition attached and a short example, so that `impact` is stored as `an impact on something` rather than as a bare noun.

examples.right: The result depends on how the sample was selected.
examples.wrong: The result depends of how the sample was selected.
examples.note: `depend on` is fixed; no other preposition follows it.

examples.right: She is responsible for three departments.
examples.wrong: She is responsible about three departments.
examples.note: `responsible for` holds whatever the translation suggests.

examples.right: Access to the archive is restricted to registered readers.
examples.note: Some nouns carry their preposition wherever they appear.

sections.heading: Adjective Plus Preposition
sections.body:
The commonest pairs fall into loose families. With `in`: `interested in`, `involved in`, `successful in`. With `of`: `aware of`, `capable of`, `typical of`, `critical of`, `guilty of`, `full of`. With `for`: `responsible for`, `suitable for`, `famous for`, `eligible for`, `grateful for`. With `to`: `similar to`, `related to`, `opposed to`, `subject to`, `accustomed to`. With `from`: `different from`, `absent from`, `derived from`. `dependent on` and `based on` take `on`.

`concerned` takes two, with different meanings: `concerned about` is worried, `concerned with` is dealing with a subject.

Every one of these prepositions is followed by an `-ing` form rather than an infinitive: `capable of measuring`, `interested in studying`, `responsible for monitoring`.

examples.right: The new figures are very similar to those published last year.
examples.wrong: The new figures are very similar with those published last year.

examples.right: Continued funding is dependent on the outcome of the review.
examples.wrong: Continued funding is dependent of the outcome of the review.

examples.right: The department was aware of the shortfall well before March.
examples.wrong: The department was aware about the shortfall well before March.

sections.heading: Verb Plus Preposition
sections.body:
Verbs with fixed prepositions form the largest group and the one that costs the most marks in writing: `depend on`, `rely on`, `insist on`, `focus on`, `consist of`, `result in`, `result from`, `contribute to`, `refer to`, `lead to`, `object to`, `account for`, `apply for`, `apply to`, `comply with`, `deal with`, `cope with`, `succeed in`, `believe in`, `suffer from` and `benefit from`.

Several take an object before the preposition: `blame someone for something`, `provide someone with something`, `remind someone of something`, `accuse someone of something`, `congratulate someone on something`, `thank someone for something`. `provide` also allows `provide something to someone`, a different arrangement of the same idea rather than an error.

`apply` shifts with its object: one applies `for` a post or a grant, and `to` an institution.

examples.right: These three factors account for roughly half of the variation.
All laboratories must comply with the revised safety code.
examples.wrong: All laboratories must comply to the revised safety code.

examples.right: The scheme provides low-income families with free travel passes.
examples.wrong: The scheme provides low-income families free travel passes.
examples.note: `provide someone with something`, or `provide something to someone`.

examples.right: She applied to three universities and for two scholarships.
examples.note: `apply to` an institution; `apply for` a post or an award.

sections.heading: Noun Plus Preposition
sections.body:
Nouns keep prepositions of their own, and they are not always those of the related verb. `discuss` takes a direct object, yet `a discussion of` or `about` a topic needs one; the verb `research` takes its object directly, while the noun takes `research into`.

The frequent pairs are `an increase in`, `a decrease in`, `a reason for`, `a need for`, `a demand for`, `an effect on`, `an impact on`, `an influence on`, `the cause of`, `the advantage of`, `a lack of`, `a solution to`, `an answer to`, `an approach to`, `an attitude towards` and `research into`.

Note the split between `in` and `on`. A quantity rises or falls `in` something, as in `an increase in rainfall`, whereas an influence is exerted `on` something, as in `an effect on rainfall`. `an increase of` is reserved for the size of the change: `an increase of twelve per cent`.

examples.right: There has been a steady increase in demand for student housing.
examples.wrong: There has been a steady increase of demand for student housing.
examples.note: `an increase in` a thing; `an increase of` introduces a figure.

examples.right: Social media has had a profound effect on political debate.
examples.wrong: Social media has had a profound effect in political debate.
examples.note: `an effect on`, `an impact on`, `an influence on`.

examples.right: The team is researching groundwater contamination.
examples.wrong: The team is researching about groundwater contamination.
examples.note: The verb takes a direct object; only the noun takes a preposition, as in `research into contamination`.

sections.heading: When the Preposition Changes the Meaning
sections.body:
Some words take more than one preposition, and the choice redirects or reverses the sense.

`result in` introduces the consequence and `result from` the cause: `The strike resulted in long delays`, but `The long delays resulted from the strike`. `agree with` applies to a person or an opinion, `agree to` to a proposal or a request, and `agree on` to a decision reached jointly. `concerned about` means worried, while `concerned with` means dealing with. `apply for` a post, `apply to` a body.

Where two prepositions are both possible, work out which relationship the sentence needs before reaching for the more familiar word.

examples.right: The reform resulted in a sharp fall in waiting times.
The fall in waiting times resulted from the reform.
Residents are concerned about the noise from the site.
The second section is concerned with methodology.

sections.heading: Verbs That Need No Preposition
sections.body:
A group of high-frequency verbs takes its object directly, and adding a preposition is an error. The main ones are `discuss`, `enter`, `approach`, `emphasise`, `mention`, `answer`, `affect`, `lack`, `comprise`, `reach`, `join`, `resemble` and `contact`.

`discuss about` is by far the most frequent of these mistakes and one of the most visible in written English. It survives because the noun `discussion` does take `about`, and because many languages express the idea with a preposition. `The report discusses the causes` is correct; `discusses about the causes` is not.

Two further contrasts are worth fixing: `affect` takes no preposition while the noun phrase `have an effect on` requires one, and `comprise` takes no preposition while `consist of` does.

examples.right: The chapter discusses the causes of urban sprawl.
examples.wrong: The chapter discusses about the causes of urban sprawl.

examples.right: Rising costs have affected enrolment across the sector.
examples.wrong: Rising costs have affected on enrolment across the sector.
examples.note: Use `affect something` or `have an effect on something`.

examples.right: The dataset comprises four thousand records.
examples.wrong: The dataset comprises of four thousand records.

examples.right: She entered the building through the side door.
examples.wrong: She entered into the building through the side door.
examples.note: `enter` a place directly; `enter into` is used only of agreements and negotiations.

slips: `discuss about` is wrong: `discuss the results`. The preposition belongs to the noun, as in `a discussion about the results`.
`depend on` and `dependent on`, never `depend of` or `depend from`.
`comply with`, `deal with` and `cope with` all take `with`, never `to`.
`an increase in` a thing, but `an increase of` a figure: `an increase in fees of eight per cent`.
`result in` gives the consequence, `result from` the cause. Check the direction before choosing.
`affect` is a verb and needs no preposition; `effect` is a noun and needs `on`.

questions.prompt: The rise in sea temperature has had a measurable effect ___ coral growth.
questions.explain: Nouns of influence take `on`: `an effect on`, `an impact on`, `an influence on`. `in` belongs to nouns of quantity, as in `an increase in temperature`.

questions.prompt: The opening chapter examines the causes ___ urban air pollution.
questions.explain: `the cause of something` is fixed, even though the verb it relates to, `cause`, takes a direct object with no preposition at all.

questions.prompt: The flooding resulted ___ two weeks of unusually heavy rainfall.
questions.explain: `result from` introduces the cause, and the rainfall is what produced the flooding. `result in` would reverse the relationship, making the flooding the cause of the rain.

questions.prompt: Exporters that fail to comply ___ the new labelling rules face heavy fines.
questions.explain: `comply with` is fixed, in the same family as `deal with` and `cope with`. `comply to` is a common transfer from the noun phrase `conformity to`.

questions.prompt: The final report consists ___ three volumes and a statistical appendix.
questions.explain: `consist of` always carries its preposition, while the near-synonym `comprise` never does.

questions.prompt: Many first-year students remain unaware ___ the support services available to them.
questions.explain: `aware of` and `unaware of` are fixed. `about` attaches to verbs and nouns of worry or discussion, not to this adjective.

questions.prompt: Higher education contributes ___ regional economic growth in several measurable ways.
questions.explain: `contribute to` is fixed, like `lead to` and `refer to`; the `to` is a preposition, so an -ing form would follow it if a verb came next.

questions.prompt: The panel will discuss ___ impact of automation on regional employment.
questions.explain: `discuss` is transitive and takes its object directly. `about` is possible only with the noun, as in `a discussion about the impact`.

questions.prompt: The university reported a sharp increase ___ the number of postgraduate applicants.
questions.explain: `an increase in` names the thing that grows; `an increase of` would have to be followed by the size of the rise, such as a percentage.

questions.prompt: The closing chapter is concerned ___ the ethics of collecting data from minors.
questions.explain: `concerned with` means deals with, which is what a chapter can do. `concerned about` means worried, a state available only to people.

questions.prompt: The site manager was blamed ___ the delay, although the fault lay with the supplier.
questions.explain: The pattern is `blame someone for something`, with the preposition before the cause; the passive keeps `for` in place.

questions.prompt: Most economists now agree ___ the authors that the tax is regressive.
questions.explain: `agree with` is used before a person or an opinion. `agree to` would need a proposal as its object, and `agree on` a jointly reached decision.
